newsitem.title: HUNGARY: E.Europe markets mixed in post-Easter week.
newsitem.headline: E.Europe markets mixed in post-Easter week.

text.p: A fall on Wall Street in the post-Easter week pushed Hungarian and Polish prices lower, but failed to impress other bourses in the region.
Prague and Bratislava were sluggish, mostly due to thinner foreign interest and Croatian shares recovered at the end of the week after dull trading earlier.
The Slovenian market rose and Bucharest picked up mostly on the back of busier activity in high-caps.
The Central European Share Index (CESI) of 73 selected Czech, Polish, Hungarian, Slovak and Slovenian stocks, fell by 0.77 percent on the week to 1,534.03 points.
PRAGUE
The Czech market was hit by continued bearish sentiment throughout the week, with most major issues moving lower.

The index's biggest issue, SPT Telecom, which accounts for 21 percent of the PX50's capitalisation, lost 100 crowns to 3,350 after posting 1996 losses of 483 million crowns, according to international accounting standards.

Radek Vavra of Citicorp Securities said the downbeat mood was caused by disappointing results from some major issues and the longstanding problem of inadequate capital market regulation which has frightened away foreign investors.
WARSAW
Polish shares tumbled by 6.1 percent this week on the back of recent drops at Western bourses, but analysts said the market, currently at 15,670.2 points, could begin to stabilise.

"I think prices have reached a corrected level in relation to the very high level that was," said Tomasz Berent of IB Austria Securities, referring to the bourse's three-year February 18 high of 18,339.4 points.
Analysts said there was a chance that if Friday's U.S. jobless data showed high employment and caused Dow falls due to expected interest rate rises, Warsaw stocks might fall again.
BUDAPEST
Hungarian share prices closed lower this week, affected by Wall Street's losses, lowering the BUX index to 5,315.46 on Friday, 98.24 points down on the week.
While the Dow's tumble left its impact on the Hungarian market, analysts found encouraging signs as well.

"On the other hand investors sold a lot, not only in Hungary, not only in the region but practically everywhere... this means that many funds are sitting on cash equivalent to as much as 30 percent (of the portfolio)," said Gabor Sitanyi, analyst at ING Barings in London.
"This is encouraging...as they have to spend it sometime."
BRATISLAVA
The Bratislava Stock Exchange was further plagued by low liquidity due to waning interest among foreign investors. Brokers saw no quick reversal of the sluggish mood.
The official 16-share SAX index firmed to 207.39 on Friday from 207.02 at Tuesday's opening.

Brokers said some shares were undervalued compared to similar issues in the region. Even blue chips like Slovnaft or drug maker Slovakofarma lacked liquidity, a likely further brake on foreign investors.
ZAGREB
Croatian stocks rebounded on Friday, ending the mixed week on a positive note thought to herald a long-awaited recovery.
"Everyone is waiting till after (local April 13) elections to start trading again," said one analyst, adding that imminent profit announcements for fully-listed firms might cap the downward trend.
Zagrebacka Banka regained five kuna to 1,800, 50 down from last week's close. Pliva slipped 10 kuna to 440 after staying off the market on Thursday.
LJUBLJANA
Slovenian shares climbed 4.62 percent this week, with the blue-chip SBI index up 58.84 points to 1,333.14.
Financial consultancy Primofin was the biggest gainer, while financial consultancy Dadas led decliners.
BUCHAREST
Growing volumes in the Bucharest bourse's two first-tier stocks hoisted turnover to around 9.0 billion lei in the week's three sessions from some 8.3 billion previously.
Heavyweight fertiliser maker Azomures and Oltchim chemical plant took the bulk of turnover and drifted higher on Thursday under buying pressure.
